description: We are satellite operations engineers working on LEO and GEO missions from the manufacturing side. We know how spacecraft are built and flown, and we joined to learn the other half: processing payload data and turning it into useful applications. We bring systems and operations know-how. We're looking for teammates with remote sensing, data science, GIS or design skills who'd like to see the mission from the hardware side too.
summary: Hotspot Harmonizers turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections over Argentina into one continuous monthly record of burning activity, so the series no longer jumps when the sensors change. MODIS (2000→) and VIIRS (2012→) see the same fires very differently: for every MODIS hotspot VIIRS reports up to 5–10, and the number of VIIRS satellites went from one to three. Adding them up produces fake "record years". We rebuild what Aqua-MODIS would have counted from VIIRS. We keep only the VIIRS detections bright enough for Aqua to see them, given the size of Aqua's pixel at that place and day. We scale each VIIRS satellite separately and average them, never sum them. We compared 34 methods with five out-of-sample tests on 14 years of overlap. Every estimate carries a 90 % uncertainty band, and that band held the truth in 88 % of the months the model never saw. The result is a public web app (hotspot-harmonizers.site): draw any area of Argentina and get a fire calendar from 2000 to today, with the current month compared against past years.
details:
What it does

- A harmonized monthly series 2000→today, split into day and night, for any area of Argentina

(drawn polygon, coordinates or study zone).

- A fire calendar: monthly counts or anomalies against the usual month.

- The current, partial month compared with the same days of earlier years, using near-real-time data marked as provisional.

- A harmonized/raw switch to show what the correction changes.

- CSV and calendar image downloads, and a leaderboard of every method we tested.

How it works

- Target: the monthly count Aqua-MODIS would have made. Aqua is the reference because it passes at about the same time as VIIRS. Terra extends 2000–2002.

- Data: 7.1 M FIRMS detections, quality-controlled. We filter by confidence and fire type, and mask static sources such as industry and gas flares.

- Final model (aqua_view_ratio_log): one ratio per VIIRS satellite, zone, day/night and period. It counts only VIIRS detections with FRP above a floor that grows with Aqua's pixel size: about 1 km at nadir, up to about 2 × 4.8 km at the swath edge. The pixel size is rebuilt from Aqua's 16-day ground track. At night Aqua sees only about 5 % of what VIIRS sees, the most intense fires, and this floor captures that.

- Uncertainty: the band comes from out-of-sample errors, by day/night and by fire size.

How we validated it

- Five tests, all out of sample: leave one year out, leave one zone out, a simulated MODIS retirement in 2019, a break test on the series, and agreement on extreme months.

- Comparison: 34 methods and 222 combinations, from simple ratios to overpass-level GLMs, GOES-East corrections and ecoregion zones.

- Result: the final model has the lowest error, and the best methods pass 2 of the 5 tests.

- External check: the yearly series follows the burned area the provinces report (Spearman r 0.86–0.89 in Córdoba and Entre Ríos).

Limits we state openly

- Since 2023 Aqua passes about 50 minutes later. We document this drift and carry it in the band, but we don't correct it.

- The model is fitted on five Argentine fire regimes and would need recalibrating for other regions.

- We count hotspots, not fires confirmed on the ground.

Why it matters: fire managers, researchers and journalists can tell whether a season is really unusual or only looks that way because the satellites changed.

Tools: Python (pandas, DuckDB, H3, statsmodels), FastAPI, React, Docker, Google Cloud. The code, methods and full results are open on GitLab, including a decision log and a method catalog.
